title: The city of eleven gates
theme: The body is a city with eleven gates belonging to the unborn one; one who attends to him does not grieve and, freed, is freed. This is that.

words.context: Śaṅkara: the body is a city, «शरीरं पुरम्»; Raṅgarāmānuja: «शरीराख्यं पुरं»
Śaṅkara counts the openings of the body: «सप्त शीर्षण्यानि, नाभ्या सहार्वाञ्चि त्रीणि, शिरस्येकम्»; Raṅgarāmānuja: the eleven senses as the gates, «एकादशेन्द्रियलक्षणबहिर्निर्गमद्वारोपेतं»
Śaṅkara: the self free of birth and change, «जन्मादिविक्रियारहितस्यात्मनो राजस्थानीयस्य»; Raṅgarāmānuja: the discerning individual self, «विवेकिन आत्मनः»; Madhva: the Lord, «अजस्येदं पुरमिति»

words.meaning: having attended to, having taken up
words.context: Śaṅkara: «अनुष्ठाय ध्यात्वा», having meditated; Raṅgarāmānuja: «विविच्य जानन्», knowing it as distinct; Madhva: «स्थितिं कृत्वा», having settled [the conviction]

words.role: main verb of the first clause

words.gram: past passive participle, m. nom. sg.
words.role: subject of vimucyate, with a prior state
words.context: Śaṅkara: freed here and now from the bonds of desire and action, «इहैवाविद्याकृतकामकर्मबन्धनैर्विमुक्तो भवति»

words.role: main verb of the second clause
words.context: Śaṅkara: «पुनः शरीरं न गृह्णातीत्यर्थः», he does not take a body again

sandhi.rule: Two like vowels merge into the long vowel, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः).
The visarga becomes s before a voiceless consonant, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः), and s becomes ś before c, P. 8.4.40 (स्तोः श्चुना श्चुः).
A final t becomes d before a voiced sound, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).

samasa.meaning: that which has eleven gates: the city of the body

samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (its first member a nañ-tatpuruṣa, न वक्रम्)
samasa.meaning: one whose thought is not crooked

morphology.note: anu-√sthā with the absolutive suffix -ya, used after a preverb: ‘having stood by, having attended to’. The s of sthā is retroflex after anu. What the attending is, the commentators decide differently (see the word table).
The present passive of vi-√muc. With the participle vimuktaḥ of the same root, the line says that one already freed is freed: two moments of one release.

translation.literal: Having attended to the eleven-gated city of the unborn one, whose thought is not crooked, one does not grieve; and, freed, one is freed. This truly is that.
translation.readable: The body is a city of eleven gates belonging to the unborn one, whose awareness never bends. Whoever attends to him grieves no more; already free, he is set free. This is that.

anvaya: अजस्य अवक्रचेतसः एकादशद्वारम् पुरम् अनुष्ठाय न शोचति । विमुक्तः च विमुच्यते । एतत् वै तत् ।
syntax: The absolutive anuṣṭhāya, with its object puram and the genitives ajasya avakracetasaḥ naming the city’s owner, comes before na śocati; the one who attends is not named. The second clause sets the participle vimuktaḥ beside the finite vimucyate of the same root. The refrain etad vai tat closes the verse, as in vallī 2.1.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the unborn, changeless self, the king of the city, whom one meditates on as its lord, «तं परमेश्वरं पुरस्वामिनम् अनुष्ठाय ध्यात्वा». Raṅgarāmānuja: the discerning individual self, who knows the body as distinct from himself, «अविवेकिनस्तु देह आत्मैव भवतीति भावः». Madhva: the city belongs to the Lord, «इदं पुरं भगवदधीनमित्यनुष्ठाय».
Śaṅkara counts openings of the body: seven in the head, three below with the navel, one at the crown. Raṅgarāmānuja takes the gates as the eleven senses through which one goes outward.

Śaṅkara: freed here from the bonds of ignorance, desire and action, and then not taking a body again. Raṅgarāmānuja: freed while living from sorrow and passion, and at the end of the karma already begun, freed from matter after the path of light, «प्रारब्धकर्मावसाने अचिरादिना विरजां प्राप्य प्रकृतिसम्बन्धविमुक्तो भवतीत्यर्थः». Madhva cites a verse: freed first by giving up self-conceit, and chiefly freed afterwards.

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Counted as written, 16, 16 and 4 syllables: two regular half-lines; the refrain etad vai tat (4) stands outside the metre.

beginner: The second part of Death’s teaching opens with a picture. The body is like a walled city with eleven gates. Śaṅkara counts them as the body’s openings: seven in the head, the navel and two below it, and one at the crown. A city does not exist for its own sake; its gates, guards and streets serve a ruler who lives inside but is not one of its buildings. So the body serves an owner, the unborn one whose awareness never bends. One who keeps attention on that owner stops grieving and is freed. Raṅgarāmānuja reads the gates as the senses and the owner as the individual self that knows itself as distinct from the body; Madhva says the city belongs to the Lord.
analogy: Like a walled town whose gates, guards and markets all work for a ruler who lives within but is not one of its houses.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: The body is a city of eleven gates whose owner is unborn and straight in thought. One who attends to him does not grieve; freed, he is freed. This is that.

commentary.q: Śaṅkara: a new approach to the hard-to-know
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: He takes the verse as a fresh attempt at the same truth, because Brahman is hard to know, «पुनरपि प्रकारान्तरेण ब्रह्मतत्त्वनिर्धारणार्थोऽयमारम्भः, दुर्विज्ञेयत्वाद्ब्रह्मणः». The body is called a city because, like a city, it is an assembly of parts that serves a master who is not part of the assembly, «स्वात्मना असंहतराजस्थानीयस्वाम्यर्थं भवितुमर्हति». Attending means meditation grounded in right knowledge, «ध्यानं हि तस्यानुष्ठानं सम्यग्विज्ञानपूर्वकम्».

commentary.q: Raṅgarāmānuja: the discerning self and its city
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The city belongs to the discerning self, free of birth and change, «जननादिविक्रियारहितस्य ऋजुबुद्धेः विवेकिन आत्मनः»; as a city stands apart from its lord, the body is known as apart from the self. For him the release is in two stages: free of sorrow and passion while living, «जीवद्दशायाम् आध्यात्मिकादिदुःख रागद्वेषादिविमुक्त एव सन्», and free of matter at the end, citing the Brahmasūtra «'भोगेन तु इतरे क्षपयित्वाऽथ सम्पद्यते'». The refrain means that even the freed self has the supreme Self as its self, «एतन्मन्त्रप्रतिपाद्यमुक्तस्वरूपमपि, परमात्मात्मकमेव इत्यर्थः».

commentary.q: Madhva: the city is the Lord’s
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Attending is settling the conviction that the city belongs to the Lord, «इदं पुरं भगवदधीनमित्यनुष्ठाय । अजस्येदं पुरमिति स्थितिं कृत्वा». For the twofold release he cites a verse, naming no source («इति च»): one is freed first, through having no self-conceit, «विमुक्तो निरभीमानात् पूर्वमेवापरोक्षवित्», and chiefly freed afterwards, «मुख्यतो मुच्यते पश्चात् दुःखाद्याभासहानतः».

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: The same genitive ajasya names the supreme self within (Śaṅkara), the individual self that discerns itself from the body (Raṅgarāmānuja) and the Lord to whom the body belongs (Madhva). All three agree that the owner is not the city; they differ on who the owner is.

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: vimuktaḥ is a past participle and vimucyate a present passive of the same root. Read together they mark a release already true and one still taking place, which each commentator places differently in time.

advaita.text: The owner of the city is the supreme Lord, meditated on as one in all beings, «तं सर्वैषणाविनिर्मुक्तः सन्समं सर्वभूतस्थं ध्यात्वा न शोचति»; freed here, one takes no body again.

visistadvaita.text: The discerning self knows the body as distinct, «विविच्य जानन्», is freed from sorrow while living and from matter at the end; even then it has the supreme Self as its self.

dvaita.text: The city belongs to the Lord, «इदं पुरं भगवदधीनमित्यनुष्ठाय»; release comes first through the loss of self-conceit and fully afterwards.

schools.disagreement: All three read the body as a city with an owner other than itself. Śaṅkara and Madhva make the owner the supreme Lord; Raṅgarāmānuja makes him the discerning individual self, whose own self is the supreme. They agree that release has two moments, now and later.

parallels.note: The Gītā uses the same image of the embodied one dwelling in a city, counting nine gates.

parallels.quote: स वा अयं पुरुषः सर्वासु पूर्षु पुरिशयो
parallels.note: The Bṛhadāraṇyaka explains puruṣa as the one who lies in every city (purīśaya), the body being the city.

contemporary.text: We easily speak of the body as ‘me’. The image of a city with an owner asks whether the one who notices hunger, sight and sound is the same as the streets those things travel along. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: If your body is a city, who lives in it?
reflect.deeper: Compare Śaṅkara’s count of the eleven gates with Raṅgarāmānuja’s. What changes in the teaching when the gates are senses rather than openings?
reflect.practice: For a few minutes, notice sights and sounds arriving as if through gates, and notice the one who receives them.

flags.note: The owner of the city: the supreme self (Śaṅkara), the discerning individual self (Raṅgarāmānuja) or the Lord (Madhva); the gates: openings of the body (Śaṅkara) or the senses (Raṅgarāmānuja).
